>> working with lists and arrays

string str = "Hello"
int len = STD->length(str)
STD->out(len) >> 5.0

>>changing string

str[2] = "O"
STD->out(str) >> HeOlo

>>currently broken

str[1] = "el"
STD->out(str) >> hello

>>number arrays work the same

>> Dio supports all basic binary oprators and brackets

int insert = 3

>> thanks to the brackets the result is 8.0

int a = (insert - 1 + 2) * 2

STD->out(a)

>>conditions

int s = 4
int b = 10

if (s > b)
    STD->out("S > B")
elseif (s < b)
    STD->out("S < B")
else
    STD->out("S = B")
end

>> STD is namespace of Standard Library functions
>> Function out takes any input that will be printed to the console

STD->out("Hello, World!")

>> loops

int c = 5
while (c > 0) >>checks is c is bigger than 0
    STD->out(c) >> 5.0, 4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0
    c -= 1 >> short for c = c - 1
end

STD->out("-----")

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i+++) >>i+++ is the same as i = i + 1
    STD->out(i)
end

>>note i++ is just i + 1 without the =

>*
All funtions have namespaces, as we used the length or out
we used "STD->out" where the STD is the namespaces
namespaces before the -> has to be passed when we are in
different namespaces (well, because we haven't defined
any namespace we technically were in STD and didn't need
to use the STD-> but it's bad practice). Namespaces are
defined with middle-processor with command:
*<

>>this creates namespace nm

def public func(int : a)::void

>*
functions are defined with keyword def then you can say public / private
if you say nothing it's by default public which means it can be called from
other namespaces (private can only be called from the same namespace)

intputs are defined by 'type : name', nire can be defined in the same
way separated by commans

possible types:
 int (arrays and int)
 string (string only)
 any (all types, string, num etc.)
